aws::graph::propositions: Semiconductor Incentives and Taiwan's Microchip Manufacturing Dominance
It amends legislation and appropriates funding for semiconductor incentives originally in the National Defence Authorization Act for 2021.
The legislation is based on eligibility requirements and prohibitions that companies should consider as they pursue incentive funding to expand domestic semiconductor manufacturing.
Analysts are concerned that the act does not address security issues, such as the Chinese government's heavy subsidies and state-sponsored cyber-espionage.
Taiwan is the world's largest microchip manufacturer, producing 65% of the microchips used globally.
The United States produces 10% of the world's microchips, and China produces 5%.
South Korea and Japan produce the remaining microchips.
Taiwan manufactures 90% of the world's advanced microchips.
The world's dependence on Taiwan's microchips has protected Taiwan from potential invasion or trade sanctions from China.

text:
It amends legislation and appropriates funding for semiconductor
incentives originally in the National Defence Authorization Act (“NDAA”) for 2021 (117th Congress
Public Law, 2022). It is based on eligibility requirements and prohibitions that companies should take
into account as they consider pursuing incentive funding to expand domestic manufacturing in the
semiconductor supply chain (King&Spalding, 2022). Analysts are concerned that the act does not
address security issues, such as the Chinese government’s heavy subsidies as well as state-sponsored
cyber-espionage (Lohman, 2022).
TAIWAN'S SUPREMACY IN MANUFACTURING MICROCHIPS
Taiwan is the world’s largest microchip manufacturer, manufacturing 65 percent of the microchips
used in everything from smartphones to missiles. This is compared to the US at 10 percent and China
at 5 percent, whereas South Korea and Japan produce the rest. 
More importantly, Taiwan manufactures 90 percent of the world’s advanced microchips. However,
the world’s dependence on Taiwan’s chips has protected itself from a potential invasion or trade
sanctions from China (Zeiger, 2022).
